newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Afghan Taleban government seeks world recognition.
newsitem.headline: Afghan Taleban government seeks world recognition.

text.p: The Islamic Taleban militia government on Sunday appealed for world recognition of its rule in Afghanistan after its sweeping weekend victories and capture of most of the country, a Taleban diplomat said.

Maulvi Shahabuddin Dilawar, Afghanistan's ambassador to Pakistan, told reporters in Islamabad that Taleban sought world recognition minutes before Pakistan became the first country to formally recognise the Taleban government in Kabul.

"The present government in Afghanistan is Islamic and a national government of Afghanistan," Dilawar said. "It should be recognised as a legal represenative of the people of Afghanistan by the world community and the other countries," he added.

"We, therefore, urge the countries of the world, especially the Islamic countries, neighbouring countries, and... Pakistan in particular, to recognise officially the government in Afghanistan before the other countries do," he added.

A Pakistan-based Afghan news service quoted a Taleban spokesman in the southern Afghan town of Kandahar, Abdul Wakil, as urging neighbouring countries not to shelter fleeing Afghan opposition figures responsible for killings.

Iran, Turkey, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan and other regional states held back from recognising the Taleban when it captured the capital Kabul last September and then fanned out to control most of the country.
Dilawar said after the latest Taleban victories those countries which would not recognise its government were not interested in stopping bloodshed in Afghanistan.
"Those countries who do not intend to recognise our government, I think they are doing injustice not only to the Islamic movement of Taleban but the people of Afghanistan."
Dilawar said his government could assure all neighbours the Taleban would not interfere in their internal affairs and meet all international obligations.
The former Soviet republics of Central Asia, alarmed by the rise of Moslem fundamentalism, hastily beefed up their border security on Sunday after advances by the Taleban.

Tajikistan, Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan are worried that the Taleban's capture on Saturday of the main northern Afghan city of Mazar-i-Sharif, former stronghold of opposition chief General Abdul Rashid Dostum, could upset regional stability. Dostum enjoyed support from the Central Asian republics.

"We urge Uzbekistan to stop interference in the internal affairs of our country and we gave assurance to that country that we will never intend to go beyond their borders, therefore we will not harm their interests," Dilawar said.
"We also demand Russia and Tajikistan to stop interfering in the internal affairs of our country and remind the bitter experiences of the history in the past."
